items.title: The Terror killed around 17,000 by guillotine — and many more by other means
items.claim: What was the human cost of the French Revolutionary Terror (September 1793-July 1794)?

options.text: Around 17,000 official executions (16,594 verified by Donald Greer), plus tens of thousands killed in the Vendée civil war and many more dying in prisons

items.reveal:
Donald Greer's 1935 study 'The Incidence of the Terror' counted 16,594 official executions. The Vendée counter-revolution and its suppression killed perhaps 170,000-250,000. Around 200,000 were imprisoned during the Terror; thousands died in custody.

Robespierre fell on 9 Thermidor Year II (27 July 1794) and was guillotined the next day — the wave he had ridden turned. The guillotine had been adopted in 1792 as a humane, egalitarian execution method.

The Bourbon Restoration (1814) and Napoleon III's regime committed their own political killings; the Paris Commune's suppression (1871) killed perhaps 10,000-20,000 in a week.
items.why: Death tolls determine how a revolution is remembered. The Terror's official 17,000 was orders of magnitude smaller than the Vendée suppression — but the urban, named victims shape memory.

items.title: The Glorious Revolution was a Dutch invasion
items.claim: William of Orange landed in Devon on 5 November 1688. How large was the force?

options.text: A diplomatic mission of a few hundred men
Around 15,000 troops on 463 ships — larger than the Spanish Armada
Only James II's English defectors, no foreign troops
A small English army recruited in advance by Parliament

items.reveal:
Seven English nobles (the 'Immortal Seven') invited William in June 1688. He landed at Brixham, Devon, with 15,000-21,000 Dutch troops, plus thousands of horses and 50 cannon. James II's army melted; key officers (including John Churchill, the future Duke of Marlborough) defected.

James fled to France in December. The Convention Parliament (January 1689) declared the throne vacant and offered it to William and Mary. The Bill of Rights followed in December 1689.

The Williamite War in Ireland (Boyne 1690) and the Highland war in Scotland (Killiecrankie 1689) were anything but bloodless.
items.why: The 'Glorious Revolution' as bloodless English self-determination is a Whig myth. It was a foreign-backed coup with extensive bloodshed in Ireland and Scotland — successful, but not peaceful.

items.title: Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170

options.text: Becket died of natural causes during a service

Four knights of Henry II — Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, Richard le Breton — murdered Archbishop Becket in Canterbury Cathedral after Henry's outburst 'Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?'
He was executed for treason after a public trial

items.reveal:
Becket and Henry had clashed for years over the jurisdiction of church courts (Constitutions of Clarendon, 1164). Becket had fled to France, returned in 1170, and excommunicated bishops who had supported Henry. The king's exact words are disputed but the four knights took them as licence.

Becket was canonised in 1173. Henry II did public penance at Canterbury in 1174, walking barefoot and being scourged by monks. The shrine became one of medieval Europe's major pilgrimage sites — the setting of Chaucer's 'Canterbury Tales' (1380s).

Henry VIII destroyed the shrine in 1538 during the Dissolution.
items.why: Church-state conflict was the defining political question of high medieval Europe. Becket's murder dramatised the limits of royal power over the church — and made Canterbury a centre of European devotion for 350 years.
